newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Thai refiners cut output in export squeeze.
newsitem.headline: Thai refiners cut output in export squeeze.

text.p: Thailand's oil refiners have cut production because of intense domestic competition and poor export returns, industry sources said on Thursday.

An official at Bangchak Petroleum Plc said the refineries were fighting to keep domestic market share against two new plants which opened earlier this year and increased imports of petroleum products by independent suppliers.
"We try to run at maximum, but sometimes it's not possible because of the economics," the Bangchak offical said.
The cutbacks are another sign of increased competition in the Asian refining sector, where production capacity is rising to meet the booming growth in demand.
South Korea is increasing refining capacity to 2.44 million bpd this year from 1.88 million barrels per day (bpd). Thailand has added 275,000 bpd this year to take its capacity to 860,000 bpd.
This is putting profit margins under pressure as refiners compete for sales.
Bangchak Petroleum has cut output at its 120,000 barrel per day (bpd) crude distillation unit (CDU) to 100,000 bpd, an official said. He declined to be named.

An industry source said the new Rayong Refinery Co had shaved output by 15,000 bpd at its 145,000 bpd CDU at Rayong on the eastern seaboard, a 60-40 joint venture between the Royal Dutch/Shell Group and the state-owned Petroleum Authority of Thailand (PTT).
Thai Oil Co, the largest refiner, cut output at its 220,000 bpd refinery due to three weeks of maintenance work on a 40,000 bpd CDU in early September.
Industry sources said a third Thai refiner, Star Petroleum Co, had cut output at a new 130,000 bpd unit by about 10,000 bpd. Star is a 60-40 joint venture between Caltex and PTT.
Esso Thailand, part of the Exxon group, said its 170,000 bpd crude units were at 95 percent capacity.
Thai Petrochemical Industry, however, was operating its small 65,000 bpd unit at full capacity, a company official said.
Refineries earn profits by buying crude oil at lower prices than the value of the products they produce.
Oil traders said international petroleum product prices were very strong, but Thai refiners were being squeezed in export markets by competitors in South Korea and Singapore.
Thai oil products were not competitive against South Korea for sales to energy-hungry China for the simple reason that South Korea is closer and freight costs are less, a trader said.
And for Thai products to sell into the Singapore market, they had to be priced under Singapore prices to make up for the freight cost, he said.
"Thai refiners pay more for their crude oil than Singapore refiners and yet their products are sold at below Singapore prices," a Singapore refiner said.
"It just does not make sense for them to export right now," said another.

One industry source said a Thai refiner had agreed to export 15,000-20,000 tonnes per month of gasoline for two years at an unusually large discount of 95 cents per barrel under market prices in Singapore -- Asia's major products market.
Other oil products, such as diesel and fuel oil, have been exported sporadically at about 50 cents per barrel and $1.00 per tonne below Singapore spot quotes.
